A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SENSEI research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

before.justification: V1 reports original MiniHack and Robodesk experiments, downstream task learning, and ablations of semantic rewards, annotation sources, and exploration weighting.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and reports additional Pokémon Red evaluations, Robodesk downstream learning, and second-generation reward-refinement results.

M1.justification: V2 substantially extends the fixed, task-free pipeline with task-conditioned VLM comparisons and extrinsic-reward integration (Section 4.4; Appendices A.1 and D.4). It also implements a second annotation and distillation round using SENSEI-collected observations (E.9), which v1 only suggested as future work. The underlying RSSM, distillation architecture, and switching mechanism remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds Pokémon Red, covering navigation, battles, Pokémon collection, and progress toward the first Gym. It retains MiniHack and Robodesk and adds the half-open-drawer task used in Robodesk downstream evaluation. This substantially broadens the evaluated environments and task requirements.

E2.justification: The original comparison sets are retained. V2 adds a from-scratch DreamerV3 control for Robodesk block-pushing (Figure 22) and evaluates a task-reward-augmented Plan2Explore comparator in Pokémon Red. These are limited extensions of existing comparator families.

E3.justification: New protocols include 750k-step Pokémon comparisons with extrinsic rewards, a large RSSM, scheduled episode lengths, and map/battle metrics. Robodesk downstream evaluation uses models pretrained through 1M exploration steps. The refinement study adds 50k annotated pairs and 200 continuation episodes with original-reward and longer-running Plan2Explore controls. These additions do not establish reruns of the retained experiments.

E4.justification: V2 retains the original ablations and adds substantial Pokémon analyses: exploration allocation across catching, leveling, and navigation (E.8), concrete reward failures in unseen locations, and a controlled continuation examining reward refinement versus longer training (E.9; Figures 26–27). These investigate additional mechanisms and failure conditions.

E5.justification: V2 adds explicit five-seed reporting for Pokémon and ten-seed reporting for Robodesk downstream learning. It also identifies the refinement demonstration as one continued SENSEI seed with a selected Plan2Explore seed, without aggregate uncertainty. Existing experiments retain their seed counts and standard-error or standard-deviation conventions; no increased replication of those experiments is established.

E6.justification: V2 adds Robodesk learning curves showing faster learning with SENSEI-pretrained models, with incomplete success on Lift-Ball (Figure 21). Pokémon results show stronger navigation and leveling, but greater catching diversity for Plan2Explore. The single-seed refinement study reports two Gym victories, first occurring around 1.8M steps. These are new results under added settings, not improvements to the retained MiniHack or Robodesk exploration scores.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 revises the mathematical reward definition in Equation 8 by adding an extrinsic-reward term controlled by chi, distinguishing task-free and task-based exploration. The existing dynamics and switching equations remain unchanged; neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and three introductory contributions retain their meaning. V2 extends the concluding account to Pokémon and changes iterative reward refinement from a future possibility into a claimed demonstrated reduction of out-of-distribution errors. It also removes the introduction's blanket assertion that prior approaches fail to transfer knowledge to novel states.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's occlusion and initial-data limitations, v2 explains how unseen regions undermine semantic rewards and leave exploration dependent on uncertainty. It interprets Pokémon behavior as influenced by the Brock-specific prompt, favoring Squirtle training over collection diversity, and explains refinement as correcting that distributional limitation. These materially expand the account of applicability and behavioral tradeoffs.

D1.justification: V2 explicitly provides a code-and-VLM-MOTIF-checkpoint link and documents Pokémon implementation details, including PokeGym version, observations, actions, frame skipping, reward modifications, starting checkpoint, hyperparameters, and annotation prompts. It also specifies the additional annotation data and continuation procedure. Most existing implementation and computational-cost disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds Pokémon-related references to Pleines et al., Suarez, and Whidden, and positions its screen-only observations against previous Pokémon agents (C.3). It narrows the introductory criticism of prior methods' transfer capabilities. The broader positioning relative to MOTIF, Plan2Explore, and RL-VLM-F remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 locally condenses the introduction, related work, captions, and discussion while retaining most existing prose and the main section sequence. Prompting becomes Appendix D, extended results move to E, and computation becomes F. These are limited editorial and organizational changes alongside the added scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the visual presentation with Pokémon maps, screenshots, progress plots, distributions, refinement comparisons, and Robodesk downstream curves. Figure 4 gains a Pokémon trajectory, Figure 7 becomes narrower, the hyperparameter table gains a Pokémon column, and the previously separate left-camera illustration is merged into Figure 9. Existing analyses are also relocated.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important evidential gap: downstream usefulness, previously demonstrated only in MiniHack, is now tested across robotic tasks with ten-seed results (Figure 21). Pokémon evaluations and explicit reward-failure analyses further strengthen understanding of the method's capabilities and limits, alongside improved reproducibility documentation. The goal-specific Pokémon prompt and single-seed refinement success constrain generalization, but the broader controlled evidence provides a substantial net improvement.
